Passive aggression is a great tool for manipulation and allows one to be petty and vindictive in some glorious ways that are particularly effective against authority figures in bureaucratic settings. However, if this is one's default coping strategy for conflict, you are going to have a hard time building relationships with normal people.

There are times for it and there are times for it not.

My landlord is really passive aggressive. He'll come into the kitchen while you're there, and if he doesn't like something you're doing (I stacked all his cast iron pans he left all over the stove once) he'll just stand there and shake his head. Or he'll wait until you step out of the room for a minute and write a nasty note. So one day I finally bitched him out about how he always leaves like 6 greasy pans all over the stove (there are 8 people living in this house) so he now keeps them elsewhere. Well, this morning I left my pan on the stove to cool down after I was done cooking (I always put it away) and when I came back 5 minutes later, my still hot cast iron pan was sitting on the cold stainless steel counter with a note: "so I guess the rules don't apply to everyone in this house."

I have a lot of other stories.

I employ it as part of covert retaliation from time to time, however. Every so often he'll get a check in the mail and I'll slip it into the "wrong address" mail and it'll get sent back. Or a snippy response will get left to his rude notes and all of the tenants will deny having written it. Or things will mysteriously go missing, only to show up in strange places later (this one really drives him nuts). Or he'll schedule a house meeting and we'll all make sure we have other prior commitments, and leave him with a headache trying to coordinate 8 separate schedules.

Passive aggressive makes no friends.

Is it alright? In moral or ethical sense? Sure. In a logical sense? No, at least not as a man.

If something isn't wrong enough to warrant clear and direct disagreement, then showing frustration passive aggressively will appear as a weak move on your part. Its like you're trying to make a play without really putting chips on the table.

I would say no.

There might be times (I can't think of any, but that doesn't preclude the possibility that there are some) at which it's the least destructive alternative available, but even that doesn't make it "all right." It just makes it least bad. And in any situation in which there's a better alternative available (which I would argue to be pretty much any situation at all), the mere fact that there's a better alternative available means that it's the wrong choice, and therefore not "all right."
